summary: A GitHub OAuth app lets your users authorize your agent, through Composio or directly, to act on their GitHub repositories and account with the scopes you request. GitHub has no app review gate, so what decides your effort is organization data: new organizations block unapproved OAuth apps by default, and each customer organization's owner must approve your app before the agent can see private org repos.

verdict.headline: No GitHub review. Register in about 15 minutes and any GitHub user can connect today, but each customer org's owner has to approve the app before we can see their private org repos.
verdict.timeToFirstConnection: Minutes on Composio's managed app. Roughly 15–30 minutes with your own OAuth app. This is our estimate; GitHub publishes no figure.
verdict.timeToProduction: Same day for personal-account data. Private organization data depends on each org owner approving your app, which can take hours to never and is outside your control.
verdict.activeEffort: 0.5–1 hour for a basic OAuth app. Several more hours if you choose the optional GitHub Marketplace listing. Both are our estimates.
verdict.approvalWait: None from GitHub (inferred: no review step appears in the docs). Per-organization owner approval is separate and has no SLA.

composio.guidance: Composio has a managed GitHub app, so you can build and test today without registering anything. Switch to your own OAuth app before production if you want any of these: your name and branding on the consent screen, custom scopes, your own rate-limit headroom (rate-limit increases are granted per OAuth app), or org owners approving an app with your name on it. Org access restrictions probably apply to the managed app too, so it won't avoid the org-approval problem. We couldn't confirm whether Composio's managed integration is an OAuth app or a GitHub App.

prerequisites.item: A GitHub account. A free one works.
prerequisites.why: The app registration page requires sign-in. The docs mention no paid plan or business account.

prerequisites.item: Admin rights on the GitHub organization, if you want the app owned by an org rather than your personal account
prerequisites.why: OAuth apps can be registered under a personal account or under any organization you administer.

prerequisites.item: A homepage URL for your product
prerequisites.why: Homepage URL is a required field on the registration form.

prerequisites.item: A Composio auth config for GitHub, so you have the exact callback URL
prerequisites.why: The callback URL registered on GitHub must match the one Composio sends.

stages.title: Register the OAuth app
stages.goal: An OAuth app exists under your account or org, with a Client ID and client secret in hand.

steps.text: Decide whether the app will be owned by your personal account or by your organization.
steps.detail: An org-owned app needs you to be an org admin, and it survives individual staff leaving. Each user or org can own up to 100 OAuth apps.

steps.text: Sign in to GitHub and open the new OAuth app form.
steps.detail: Personal account: https://github.com/settings/applications/new (it redirects to sign-in if you're logged out). For an org-owned app, open the OAuth apps section of that organization's developer settings.

steps.text: Fill in Application name, Homepage URL and Application description.
steps.detail: An agent can draft the name and description. Homepage URL is required; description is optional. Users see the app name on the consent screen, so use your product name.

steps.text: Enter the Authorization callback URL from your Composio auth config.
steps.detail: Expected value: https://backend.composio.dev/api/v3.1/toolkits/auth/callback. Copy the exact value from your Composio dashboard rather than trusting this one. GitHub allows up to 10 callback URLs, so you can also add an older Composio v3 callback if you need it.

steps.text: Decide whether to leave 'Expire user access tokens' checked.
steps.detail: The creating-an-app doc says it is on by default, which gives 8-hour tokens plus a refresh token. Another GitHub doc calls OAuth tokens long-lived by default, so look at the checkbox yourself. Keep it checked only if Composio or your code refreshes tokens.

steps.text: Leave 'Enable Device Flow' unchecked unless you need CLI or device login.
steps.detail: Optional toggle. It isn't needed for a browser-based Composio connection.

steps.text: Click Register application, copy the Client ID, then generate and save a client secret.
steps.detail: Store the secret in your secrets manager straight away. The token endpoint is https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token and the authorize endpoint is https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize. There is no OIDC discovery document.

stages.title: Configure scopes and Composio
stages.goal: Composio is using your Client ID and secret with a minimal scope list and a callback that matches exactly.

steps.text: Write the minimal scope list for what your agent actually does.
steps.detail: Start from the narrowest scopes that work: no scope gives public read-only access, user:email reads email addresses, repo:status covers commit statuses, read:repo_hook covers webhooks. Use 'repo' only if you need private repo read/write. Scopes never grant more than the user already has.

steps.text: In Composio, set your GitHub auth config to use your own credentials (Client ID, client secret, scopes).
steps.detail: An agent can prepare the values. You must sign in to the Composio dashboard and paste the secret yourself.

steps.text: Check that the callback URL on GitHub matches Composio's exactly, character for character.
steps.detail: Check scheme, host, path (v3.1 vs v3) and any trailing slash. You must open both settings pages, because an agent can't see them without your credentials.

steps.text: Confirm token refresh is handled if token expiry is on.
steps.detail: Expiring tokens last 8 hours. Users can also opt in to expiry per sign-in through the offline_access scope. If refresh isn't handled, connections will break after 8 hours.

stages.title: Test real connections
stages.goal: Your own account connects and API calls work, and you know how org-owned repos behave.

steps.text: Connect your own GitHub account through a Composio connect link.
steps.detail: The authorize endpoint sends you to GitHub sign-in first, then to the consent screen. If you see an error page instead of consent, the client_id or callback is wrong; we couldn't observe the exact error text.

steps.text: Run a test API call against a repo you personally own.
steps.detail: For example, list your repositories. This confirms the token and scopes work.

steps.text: Try the same call against a private repo in an organization you belong to.
steps.detail: If the org has OAuth app access restrictions on (the default for new orgs), expect private org data to be missing until an org owner approves your app.

steps.text: Reconnect the same account once, then confirm the earlier connection still works.
steps.detail: GitHub keeps at most 10 tokens per user/app/scope combination and allows 10 new tokens per hour. One community report describes the earlier token being revoked on every login.

stages.title: Go live
stages.goal: Production users connect through your app, and customers know how to approve it for their orgs.
stages.duration: 15–30 min hands-on. Org approvals take indefinite time per customer. Marketplace is optional and its timeline is unknown.

steps.text: Point production connections at your own auth config.
steps.detail: GitHub has no publish step or test-user cap; any GitHub user can authorize straight away (inferred from the docs).

steps.text: Write instructions telling customers' org owners how to approve your OAuth app.
steps.detail: Explain that members can request access from the authorization flow, that owners get notified, and that until an owner approves, the agent can't read private org repos or write to the org's public repos.

steps.text: Ask each customer's org owner to approve the app, or to confirm that restrictions are off.
steps.detail: This is the customer's decision. Owners can also turn off members' ability to request approval.

steps.text: Optional: if you want discovery or billing through GitHub, prepare a GitHub Marketplace listing.
steps.detail: An agent can draft the privacy policy, description and support info. You must accept the Marketplace Developer Agreement, set pricing, add plan-change webhooks, complete publisher verification and submit; org-owned apps need an org owner to submit. The app must do more than authentication and must be publicly available. This is not required for users to connect.

steps.text: If heavy users hit rate limits, request a rate-limit increase for your OAuth app.
steps.detail: Each user's token is limited to 5,000 requests/hour and does not scale up. Increases are granted per OAuth app; we didn't find the request process.

blockers.title: Org repos missing after a successful connection
blockers.symptom: The user connects fine, but the agent can't see their company's private repos, can't write to the org's public repos, and gets no webhooks from private org repos.
blockers.workaround: Have the user request approval from the authorization flow, or send the org owner your approval instructions. The org owner must approve your OAuth app. This probably applies to Composio's managed app too.

blockers.title: SAML single sign-on organization
blockers.symptom: The token works for personal repos but can't reach an org that enforces SAML SSO.
blockers.workaround: Ask the user to sign in through the org's SSO, then retry.

blockers.title: Callback URL or client_id mismatch
blockers.symptom: After GitHub sign-in, the user sees an error instead of the consent screen. We couldn't observe the exact message because it appears behind the login wall.
blockers.workaround: Copy the callback URL from the Composio dashboard into the app's callback URL field exactly, and check that Composio has the right Client ID.

blockers.title: Earlier tokens revoked on reconnect
blockers.symptom: Older connections for the same user stop working after new connections are made across agents or environments.
blockers.workaround: Avoid needless re-authorization; reuse one connection per user. The documented cap is 10 tokens per user/app/scope. One community report describes revocation on every login, possibly tied to enterprise-managed accounts.

blockers.title: Connections break after about 8 hours
blockers.symptom: API calls start failing with authentication errors several hours after the user connected.
blockers.workaround: Make sure refresh tokens are used, or uncheck 'Expire user access tokens' on the app.

blockers.title: Rate limiting for heavy users
blockers.symptom: API calls get rate-limited after about 5,000 requests in an hour for a given user.
blockers.workaround: Batch or cache requests, or request a rate-limit increase for your own OAuth app. That isn't possible on the managed app.

nuances.text: GitHub recommends building a GitHub App instead of an OAuth app, for fine-grained permissions, per-repository user control and short-lived tokens. Consider it if org admins resist granting the broad 'repo' scope.
GitHub OAuth apps don't use OpenID Connect. There's no discovery document, and the endpoints are fixed at /login/oauth/authorize and /login/oauth/access_token.
Scopes only restrict a token; they never grant more than the user already has.
A 2020 forum answer says the token cap is 100. Current docs say 10, so trust the docs.
For a basic OAuth app you need no legal entity, payment, demo video or privacy policy. A privacy policy, pricing plan and developer agreement only come in with an optional Marketplace listing.

agentCanDo: Draft the app name and description
Write the org-owner approval instructions for customers
Draft Marketplace listing text, privacy policy and support info if you choose to list
youMustDo: Sign in to GitHub and register the OAuth app
Enter the callback URL and decide the token-expiry setting
Generate and store the client secret
Test connections with your own account
Ask customers' org owners to approve the app
Accept the Marketplace agreement and set pricing, if listing

claims.note: [Checker: confirmed in source. "When you create a new organization, OAuth app access restrictions are enabled by default."]

claims.statement: While restrictions are on, unapproved OAuth apps get no API access to private org resources, cannot create/update/delete public org resources, and get no webhook deliveries from private repos.

sources.title: About OAuth app access restrictions - GitHub Docs

claims.note: [Checker: only partly supported. The page says "API access to private organization resources is not available for unapproved OAuth apps" and "Hook deliveries from private organization repositories will no longer be sent to unapproved OAuth apps." On public resources, though, it only rules out "privileged create, update, or delete actions," not all of them. The page also notes that "Hooks created by users and hooks created before May 2014 will not be affected."]
